periods.analysis: We opened the arc in a strong position: rolling petroleum throughput stood at 133,333,565 barrels, comfortably green against the 130,000,000-barrel target. With no prior quarter in this run, I am treating 2024-Q3 as the operating baseline, not a victory lap. The South Tank Farm and the airport hydrant line both ran cleanly through the late-summer travel peak, and the Berths 8-10 sequencing team kept truck, vessel, and pipeline moves from stepping on one another. This is the kind of quiet reliability that lets a gateway city grow without making the fuel system the headline.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the current berth-window discipline by keeping the 0600 and 1800 petroleum coordination calls with pilots, terminal operators, and airport fuel consortium staff. Extend the green performance by adding a weekend relief crew for meter proving and hose inspections at Berths 9 and 10 before the winter cruise-and-air peak. I also want Operations to lock the Q3 playbook into the Port Everglades Trade Gateway dashboard so we can distinguish real demand softness from avoidable scheduling friction.

periods.analysis: The rolling total slipped to 129,570,116 barrels, down 3,763,449 from 2024-Q3, which moved us from green into yellow just below the 130,000,000 target. I am not alarmed, but I am paying attention: the miss is narrow enough to manage and large enough to respect. Two factors showed up in the logs: three weather-compressed vessel windows during king-tide weeks and a planned pump outage on Fuel Main FM-42 that pushed some product into January nominations. The team protected safety and inventory, which is non-negotiable, but the quarter reminded us that a coastal gateway does not get free capacity on rough-water days.
periods.recommendations: Keep the yellow watch-item tight around berth recovery time after tidal or weather holds, with a weekly exception report from Marine Operations until the rolling number is back above 130,000,000 barrels. Pull the FM-42 maintenance after-action into a 30-day mitigation plan, including pre-staged gaskets, spare actuators, and a second contractor crew on call for the next planned outage. Ask the terminal operators to submit January-February catch-up nominations early so we can recover volume without crowding aviation fuel deliveries.

periods.analysis: Throughput was essentially flat at 129,601,367 barrels, up 31,251 from 2024-Q4, so we stayed yellow but stopped the slide. That small gain matters because it tells me the system stabilized after the Q4 weather and FM-42 maintenance drag, but it does not yet clear the bar. The petroleum desk recovered some deferred movements through the North Gate truck rack and two additional GulfLink barge calls, while airport jet-fuel demand remained steady rather than spectacular. My read is that we are holding the line, not yet accelerating.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the yellow watch on rolling nominations versus actual liftings, with Commercial and Harbor Operations reconciling every Friday by terminal and product class. Authorize a targeted two-week overtime block for the Berth 8 manifold crew during high-confidence vessel windows, but do not normalize overtime as the operating model. Have Engineering confirm that Valve Pit VP-17 and the FM-42 bypass are ready before the spring import cycle, because we cannot afford another maintenance-related deferral.

periods.analysis: The system responded well in 2025-Q2: rolling throughput rose to 133,821,028 barrels, up 4,219,661 from 2025-Q1, returning the measure to green. That is a clean recovery above the 130,000,000 target, and it came from managed execution rather than wishful demand. The spring refinery schedule lined up with additional vessel calls at Berths 9 and 10, the airport consortium advanced two jet-fuel lifts before the summer travel surge, and the terminal dispatchers kept dwell time down on the South Tank Farm route. This is the pivot I wanted to see after two yellow quarters: disciplined capacity recovery with safety still intact.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by preserving the Q2 berth-sequencing model through the summer, especially the shared daily look-ahead for petroleum vessels, tank capacity, and airport pipeline pulls. Extend the improvement by negotiating two additional pre-cleared night windows per month with pilots and terminal security for low-conflict product movements. Capture the Q2 recovery tactics in a standard operating bulletin so the next yellow quarter triggers a known playbook, not improvisation.

periods.analysis: Rolling petroleum throughput remained green at 132,762,263 barrels, though it eased by 1,058,765 from 2025-Q2. I am comfortable with the position, because the value is still above target, but the softening deserves an early look before it becomes a pattern. The summer travel peak supported aviation fuel, while two crude-product cargoes shifted later after a vendor inspection hold on Tank 14B and a congested tug schedule during Labor Day week. In plain terms, the gateway is still moving strong volume, but our margin over the target narrowed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping the airport jet-fuel priority lane active through September closeout and protecting Berth 10 from non-petroleum encroachment during confirmed tanker arrivals. Extend capacity resilience by pre-booking tug availability for the next three holiday weeks and requiring Atlantic Tankage to provide a firm return-to-service date for Tank 14B. Watch the rolling cushion over 130,000,000 barrels; if it drops below 1,000,000 barrels, convene the petroleum recovery huddle within 48 hours.

periods.analysis: The rolling total fell to 129,282,776 barrels, down 3,479,487 from 2025-Q3, moving us back into yellow. This is the second fourth-quarter dip in the sequence, and I do not want anyone treating that as a seasonal shrug. The logs point to a familiar coastal mix: king-tide restrictions, a five-day refinery allocation cut, and longer truck turn times at the North Gate after the access-control software upgrade. We are still close to the target, but close is not green, and the watch-item is now recovery speed heading into Q1.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a 60-day yellow recovery plan with named owners for three items: berth recovery after tide holds, North Gate truck turn time, and refinery nomination shortfalls. Direct IT and Terminal Security to tune the access-control vendor settings and report average truck cycle time twice weekly until the queue is back within the port standard. Use the January nomination book to pull forward confirmed aviation and diesel volumes where storage and safety margins allow.

periods.analysis: Throughput improved slightly to 129,414,784 barrels, up 132,008 from 2025-Q4, but the measure remains yellow. The good news is that the Q4 drop did not continue; the harder news is that the recovery is still too shallow for a gateway of our scale. The North Gate software fix reduced the worst truck queues, and Berth 9 handled two clean catch-up calls, but refinery supply remained choppy and one fog closure took away a high-value tide window. We are managing the problem, but we have not yet converted management into enough barrels.
periods.recommendations: Keep the yellow recovery plan active for another quarter and make the watch-item explicit: confirmed vessel windows must translate into completed liftings within the same operating week. Add a temporary petroleum scheduler on the 1400-2200 shift for six weeks to bridge terminal, pilot, and airport consortium decisions in real time. Have Commercial secure written spring volume commitments from the top five petroleum customers so Operations can plan labor and tank turns against firm demand.

periods.analysis: This quarter delivered the break we needed: rolling petroleum throughput climbed to 135,531,515 barrels, up 6,116,731 from 2026-Q1, and returned decisively to green. That is not just back over the 130,000,000 target; it is the strongest result in this eight-quarter run. The spring volume commitments held, the added evening scheduler cleared conflicts before they hit the dock, and the airport hydrant line took sustained jet-fuel pulls without disrupting marine product moves. After two yellow quarters, the team turned a managed risk into a measurable operating win.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by making the evening petroleum scheduler permanent through the next budget quarter and tying the role to completed liftings, not just scheduled calls. Extend the gains by reserving a recurring second night window at Berth 9 for high-confidence cargoes and by keeping the customer commitment process in place for the next rolling cycle. Close the yellow recovery plan formally, but retain the tide-hold and truck-cycle dashboards as early-warning tools so we do not have to relearn this lesson in Q4.

periods.analysis: Rolling petroleum throughput eased from 135,531,515 to 133,800,000 barrels but remains above the 130,000,000 target. The smaller cushion calls for monitoring rather than a recovery declaration.
periods.recommendations: Keep the evening scheduling and tide-hold reviews in place, and check completed liftings against customer commitments.
